question_stem: Cancer cells often have reduced amounts of surface proteins, including class I MHC antigens. Which of the following cells can exploit this property to kill cancer cells?

answer_summary: Natural Killer cells (NK cells) are a class of lymphocytes which act against malignant cells and virus infected cells.
explanation_markdown:
**Natural Killer cells (NK cells)** are a class of lymphocytes which act against **malignant cells** and virus infected cells.

* Natural killer cells belong to innate immunity.
* NK cells lack antigen specific receptors and are referred to as **Large granular lymphocytes.** (LGL)
* NK cells are identified by **CD16** and **CD56** cell surface receptors.
* NK cell activity is augmented by interferons and upon activation, they release perforins and granzymes and express Fas L.

**The common feature** of both **cytotoxic T-cells and NK cells** is effectivity against **virus-infected cells.**

**The difference** is however that **cytotoxic T-cell is MHC- I restricted** while **NK cell is NK cells adapt accordingly to the presence or absence of MHC class I molecules.**

Changes in steady state MHC expression can lead to gain or loss of responsiveness in NK cells, but the inflammatory conditions associated with infections act to sustain a higher state of responsiveness, enabling initially hyporesponsive NK cells to provide protective activity, and to do so without being subject to inhibition by self MHC I molecules.

![Natural Killer Cell Mechanism](assets/images/MC2862_explanation_1.jpg)

When NK cells respond to antibodies which are bound to cancer antigens, NK cells get activated and attack them.

question_stem: Which toll-like receptor binds to the flagella of bacteria?

answer_summary: Toll-like receptor (TLR) 5 binds to the flagella of bacteria.
explanation_markdown:
Toll-like receptor (TLR) 5 binds to the flagella of bacteria.

**Toll-like receptors (TLRs)** are **type 1 transmembrane receptors** that have an extracellular domain, which detects infecting pathogens.

* **TLR 1, 2, 4, and 6** recognize **bacterial lipids**.
* **TLR 3, 7 and 8** recognize **viral RNA**.
* **TLR 9** recognizes **bacterial DNA and some herpes viruses**.
* **TLR 5 and 10** recognize bacterial or parasite **proteins**.

Upon detection of a pathogen, the intracellular domain of these receptors (**TIR domain**) initiates the activation of signaling pathways such as **NF-kappa B pathway**, which stimulates the production of co-stimulatory molecules and cytokines involved in anti-microbial defense and inflammation.

| TLR 2 | Bacterial peptidoglycan |
| TLR 3 | dsRNA of viruses |
| TLR 4 | LPS of gram-negative bacteria |
| TLR 5 | Flagella of bacteria |
| TLR 7 | ssRNA of viruses |
| TLR 9 | Bacterial DNA, Some Herpesviruses |

answer_summary: Adoptive immunity is a type of immunization in which immunologically competent lymphocytes, known as transfer factors, are injected.

**Adoptive immunity** is a type of immunization in which immunologically competent lymphocytes, known as **transfer factors**, are injected.

It is analogous to adoption: a child is once adopted out from their home, grown up, and then returned to their home of birth. Transferred immunological components include immune cells such as T lymphocytes or tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes, NK cells, macrophages, or B cells

Transfer factor has the ability to passively transfer cell mediated immunity in the recepient to those antigens to which the donor is sensitive.

* **Natural active immunity** : Clincial or subclinical infection.
* **Artificial active immunity** : Vaccination
* **Natural passive immunity** : Transplacental transfer of antibody, colustrum.
* **Artificial passive immunity:** Anti-tetanus serum, anti-diphtherial serum

question_stem: Which of the following statements is true?

options.text: No memory is seen with T cell-dependent antigen response
T cell-dependent antigen is rapidly metabolised
T cell independent antigen activates B cells monoclonally only

peer_accuracy_statement: 27% of the people got this right
answer_summary: T cell-dependent antigen is rapidly metabolised.
explanation_markdown:
T cell-dependent antigen is rapidly metabolised.

**T-cell dependant antigens (TD)**-Antigens that require **T-cell** participation for the production of immune response.

* They are structurally complex.
* They have a wide range of immunogenic dose and have immunological memory.
* **They activate only mature B cells monoclonally** and the B cells undergo affinity maturation and class switch over.
* All classes of antibodies are activated.
* They are rapidly metabolized.

**T-cell independent antigens (TI)**-Antigens which directly stimulate antibody production by **B-cells.**

* They are structurally simple.
* They have dose dependant immunogenicity and no immunological memory
* **They activate both mature and immature B cells polyclonally** and the B cells do not undergo affinity maturation and class switch over.
* The antibody response is restricted to IgM and IgG3
* They are slowly metabolized.

Super antigens cause **polyclonal activation of T cells.**

* Highly resistant to proteases and to denaturation by CD4+ T cells.

* Staphylococcal enterotoxins, TSST, Exfoliative toxin
* Streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxin
* Mycobacterium tuberculosis
* HIV nef
* CMV, EBV and rabies nucleocapsid protein

answer_summary: The secretory component of IgA is formed by epithelial cells of lining mucosa.
explanation_markdown:
The **secretory component of IgA** is formed by **epithelial cells of lining mucosa.**

**IgA** occurs in two forms- **Serum IgA** and **Secretory IgA**

**Serum IgA** is a monomer that circulates in serum.

**Secretory IgA** is a dimer formed by two monomer units joined together at their carboxy terminals by a glycopeptide known as **J - chain** and a glycine-rich polypeptide known as **secretory component (secretory piece).**

Secretory IgA along with the **J chain** is synthesized by the **plasma cells** situated near the mucosal or glandular epithelium and its **secretory component** is synthesized by **epithelial cells**, not by plasma cells.

The secretory component is believed to protect IgA from denaturation by bacterial proteases.

answer_summary: Nude mice is not resistant to xenograft due to absence of T cell.
explanation_markdown:
Nude mice is not resistant to xenograft due to absence of T cell.

Xenograft: A tissue graft or organ transplant from a donor of a different species.

Nude mice

* The phenotype of the mouse is a **lack of body hair**, which gives it the "nude" nickname. The genetic basis of the nude mouse mutation is a disruption of the **FOXN1 gene.**
* Nude mice **lacks "Thymus"** & cannot generate mature T lymphocytes.
* **Absence of T-lymphocytes** makes it unable to mount adaptive immune responses requiring CD4, helper T cells, CD8 and cytotoxic T cells.

Adaptive immune responses that remain unresponsive to nude mice include:

* Antibody formation (CD4 + helper T cells)
* Cell-mediated immune responses (CD4+ and/or CD8+ T cells)
* Delayed-type hypersensitivity responses (CD4+ T cells)
* Killing of virus-infected or malignant cells (CD8 + cytotoxic T cells)
* Graft rejection (both CD4+ & CD8+ T cells)

Application of Nude mice:

* Laboratory study animal - Insights into immune system, leukemia, solid tumors, AIDS & other immune deficiency diseases.
* Absence of functioning T cells prevents them rejecting the allografts & Xenografts.

**MARROW Pearl #509 • Microbiology: Various Types of Chemokines Based on their Structure**

The major role of chemokines is to act as a chemoattractant to guide the migration of inflammatory cells.

Members of the chemokine family are divided into four groups depending on the number and arrangement of Cysteine molecules.

**1. CXC chemokines** (or α-chemokines): They are **separated by one amino acid**, represented in this name with an "X". Eg: Interleukin -8 (CXCL8)

**2. CC chemokines** (or β-chemokines): They have total four cysteines of which **two are adjacent cysteines** (amino acids), near their amino terminus. Eg: CC chemokine ligands (CCL)-1 to 28

**4. CX3C chemokines** (or d-chemokines): They have **three amino acids between the two cysteines** and is termed CX3C chemokine (or d-chemokines). Eg: fractalkine (or CX3CL1) which acts as a chemoattractant and as an adhesion molecule.

answer_summary: This is an example of IgE mediated type of hypersensitivity reaction.
explanation_markdown:
This is an example of **IgE mediated** type of hypersensitivity reaction.

**Type 1 hypersensitivity**

* These are called allergic reactions and are induced by environmental antigens (allergens) that stimulate strong TH2 responses and IgE production in genetically susceptible individuals

2 phases of Type I reaction:

answer_summary: Eichwald-Silmser effect is a unilateral sex-linked histoincompatibility.
explanation_markdown:
**Eichwald-Silmser effect** is a unilateral sex-linked histoincompatibility.

While transplants between siblings are successful, an exception is seen when the donor is a male and the recipient a female.

Such grafts are rejected as the grafted male tissue (XY) will have antigens determined by the Y chromosome which will be absent in the female (XX) recipient.

Grafts from female to male will succeed.

answer_summary: Hyper IgM syndrome is an inherited deficiency in the CD40 ligand.
explanation_markdown:
Hyper IgM syndrome is an inherited deficiency in the CD40 ligand.

This is an X-linked disorder where T helper cells fail to express functional CD40L on their plasma membrane, which typically interacts with the CD40 molecule present on B cells and dendritic cells (DCs).

This costimulatory engagement is required for APC activation, and its absence in B cells interferes with class switching, B-cell responses to T-dependent antigens, and the production of memory cells. The B-cell response to T-independent antigens, however, is unaffected, accounting for the presence of IgM antibodies; hence, the condition is known as hyper IgM syndrome (HIM).

CD40–CD40L interactions are also required for DC maturation and IL-12 secretion; so, defects in this pathway result in increased susceptibility to intracellular pathogens.

answer_summary: Staphylococcus aureus is a gram-positive coccus found in clusters and is catalase positive and coagulase positive.
explanation_markdown:
*Staphylococcus aureus* is a gram-positive coccus found in clusters and is catalase positive and coagulase positive.

A **coccus** (plural **cocci**) is any bacterium that has a spherical, ovoid, or generally round shape. Cocci may occur as individual cells or remain attached after cell division. Those that remain attached can be classified based on the cellular arrangement as follows:

| Bacteria | Arrangement |
| :--- | :--- |
| *Staphylococcus* | Cluster |
| *Streptococcus* | Chain |
| *Pneumococcus* | Pairs/lanceolate shaped |
| *Micrococcus* | Tetrads |
| *Sarcina* | Octate |

The staphylococci grow in clusters because the cells divide successively in **3 perpendicular planes**, with the daughter cells remaining attached to one another following each successive division.

**About other options:**

**a) *Streptococcus pyogenes*** are **arranged in chains** and are catalase negative.

**c) *Staphylococcus epidermidis*** are arranged in clusters and are catalase positive and **coagulase negative.**

**d) *Neisseria meningitidis***, often referred to as meningococcus, is a **gram-negative bacterium.**

answer_summary: Protein A forms the basis of co-agglutination reaction shown by Staphylococcus aureus.
explanation_markdown:
Protein A forms the basis of co-agglutination reaction shown by *Staphylococcus aureus.*

* **Protein A** has **chemotactic, antiphagocytic,** and **anti-complementary** properties.
* Protein A binds to Fc terminal of IgG (except IgG3), leaving the **Fab terminal free** to combine with its specific antigen.
* Hence, protein A bearing staphylococci, coated with any IgG antiserum, will be agglutinated if mixed with the corresponding antigen.

* Antibiotic susceptibility test on **Muller Hilton agar (Disk diffusion test)** by using Methicillin or Oxacillin disc or cefoxitin disc.
* **PCR** for detection of mecA gene.

**Conditions to be maintained for Incubation:**
* On media containing 4% NaCl
* Incubation at 30°C
* Full 24hr incubation

**Treatment:**
* **Vancomycin** is Drug Of Choice (should be used only if other drugs are resistant ).
* Others- Teicoplanin, Linezolid, streptogramin, cipro/levofloxacin, cotrimoxazole, clindamycin, mupirocin, minocycline.
* **Newer Drugs** – Daptomycin, **ceftobiprole,** tigecycline, oritavancin,dalbavancin,telavancin,delaflo[xacin]
* **Ceftobiprole** and **ceftaroline** are 5th generation β lactams effective against MRSA.

pearls.title: Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA)
pearls.body_text:
MRSA Definition: Methicillin MIC 8 µg/ml or more, Oxacillin MIC 4 µg/ml or more.

Resistance in MRSA is mediated by mecA gene which is chromosomally coded.

It alters PBP (penicillin binding protein) present on s.aureus cell wall to PBP-2a which has less affinity for beta-lactam antibiotics.

Penicillin Binding Protein:
• Normal protein present in all bacterial cell wall.
• Transpeptidase in nature.
• Required for cross-linking of the peptidoglycan layer (essential for cell wall synthesis).
• It is also the site of attachment for- beta-lactam drugs to bind & inhibit.

Types of MRSA:
• Community-acquired - mediated by mec A subtype IV and Possess PV Toxin(Panton-Valentine Toxin), monodrug resistance,more virulent
• Hospital-acquired - mediated by mec A subtype I, II, III, multidrug resistance,less virulent.

Detection of MRSA:
• Antibiotic susceptibility test on Muller Hilton agar (Disk diffusion test) by using Methicillin or Oxacillin disc or cefoxitin disc.
• PCR for detection of mecA gene.

Conditions to be maintained for Incubation:
• On media containing 4% NaCl
• Incubation at 30°C
• Full 24hr incubation

Treatment:
• Vancomycin is Drug Of Choice (should be used only if other drugs are resistant ).
• Others- Teicoplanin, Linezolid, streptogramin, cipro/levofloxacin, cotrimoxazole, clindamycin, mupirocin, minocycline.
• Newer Drugs – Daptomycin, ceftobiprole, tigecycline, oritavancin,dalbavancin,telavancin,delaflo[xacin]
• Ceftobiprole and ceftaroline are 5th generation β lactams effective against MRSA.
